paragraphs.text: A cake of [Fujian white tea](fujian-white:definition) dated 2016. Inside is leaf that was only [withered and then dried at low heat](fujian-white:making), never fixed and never rolled. [Pressed white tea](fujian-white:cakes) is a young form: cakes began in the 2000s and spread around 2010, because a cake is smaller and easier to keep and carry than loose leaf. Some cakes are pressed from leaf already aged loose for a few years, so the year on a cake can mark the pressing rather than the pick.

At ten years it has passed the seven of the trade's saying, [one year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure](fujian-white:ageing). That is a saying, not a measure, and no agreed number of years makes a white tea aged. It is best kept dry, clean and aired, away from strong smells and sunlight.

brewing.text: Gongfu style, use about 1 gram of leaf to 15 to 25 ml of water, for example 5 grams in a 100 to 110 ml gaiwan; weigh it, since the leaf is light and bulky. Silver Needle and young, delicate tea take water below the boil, about 75 to 90°C; older, leafier or aged tea takes water at or near the boil. Start with a steep of 10 to 45 seconds and add a few seconds each round. An aged cake is often rinsed quickly first, and older pressed tea can be simmered on the stove, about 5 grams to 500 ml for 3 to 10 minutes; young, delicate tea is not.

notice.text: Jujube or dried dates, herbs and medicine, wood, honey and dried fruit, a deeper, redder liquor, a thicker, rounder body, and less lift in the scent than a young tea.
